claims.claim: IST-3 enrolled 3035 people with acute ischaemic stroke, of whom 1617 (53%) were older than 80.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "3035 patients were enrolled by 156 hospitals in 12 countries. All of these patients were included in the analyses (1515 in the rt-PA group vs 1520 in the control group), of whom 1617 (53%) were older than 80 years of age." Full text (Discussion, Scite excerpt): "For the types of patient recruited in IST-3 (about three quarters of whom were randomised after 3 h, and half of all patients were older than 80 years of age), by 6 months there was evidence that rt-PA improved functional outcome." Discussion (Scite citation snippet): "Nonetheless, the trial was the largest-ever trial of thrombolysis therapy for stroke (over three times larger than any previous trial)"
claims.location: Abstract (Findings); Discussion (Scite full-text excerpts; citation numerals omitted)
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults with acute ischaemic stroke treatable within 6 h / IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg / open control / alive and independent at 6 months / enrolled 2000-2011 in 12 countries
claims.safe_wording: IST-3, an international trial of the clot-busting drug alteplase for stroke, enrolled 3035 people. Just over half of them (1617, or 53 in 100) were over 80. About half of all participants received the drug and half did not.
claims.qualifications: Say 'enrolled' or 'took part', not 'treated': the 53% covers both the alteplase and the control groups. 'Largest-ever trial of thrombolysis for stroke' was the authors' description in 2012; later trials (for example of tenecteplase or of alteplase doses) were not checked, so do not call IST-3 'the largest' in 2026 without that qualification ('at the time, the largest').
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None on the enrolment figures.

claims.claim: Before IST-3, people over 80 had largely been excluded from trials of clot-busting treatment for stroke.
claims.supporting_passage: IST-3 Introduction (Scite citation snippets): "Older people have been under-represented in stroke trials in general, and in stroke thrombolysis trials in particular (only 79 people aged older than 80 years had been included in trials of rt-PA)." ... "Thrombolytic therapy with intravenous recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rt-PA), when approved in Europe, was restricted to the treatment of patients younger than 80 years of age with acute ischaemic stroke who could be treated within 3 h." ESO guideline (full-text excerpt): "Most trials of IVT for ischaemic stroke have excluded patients who were over 80 years old or who had multimorbidity/frailty or pre-stroke disability."
claims.location: IST-3 Introduction; ESO guideline text (Scite full-text excerpts; citation numerals omitted)
claims.pico_timeframe: Trials of IV thrombolysis for acute ischaemic stroke up to 2012 / participants over 80
claims.safe_wording: Before IST-3, trials of this clot-busting drug had included only 79 people over 80, according to the IST-3 authors. When the drug was first approved in Europe, it was licensed only for people under 80. European stroke guideline authors note that most thrombolysis trials excluded people over 80, or with frailty or disability before the stroke.
claims.qualifications: The 79 figure is background in the IST-3 introduction (citing a Cochrane review), so attribute it ('the IST-3 authors reported'). The under-80 restriction describes the original European approval, not current licensing, which was not checked.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Current licensing status of alteplase by age in the UK was not verified; do not state it.

claims.claim: Clot-busting treatment (alteplase) within the licensed time window helps people over 80 about as much, in relative terms, as younger people.
claims.supporting_passage: Emberson abstract: "We did a pre-specified meta-analysis of individual patient data from 6756 patients in nine randomised trials comparing alteplase with placebo or open control." ... "We defined a good stroke outcome as no significant disability at 3-6 months, defined by a modified Rankin Score of 0 or 1." ... "Proportional treatment benefits were similar irrespective of age or stroke severity." Emberson full text (Results, Scite excerpt): "The effect of alteplase treatment was similar for patients aged 80 years or younger (mean treatment delay 4·1 h; 990 [39%] vs 853 [34%]; OR 1·25, 95% CI 1·10–1·42, p<0·0001) and for those older than 80 years (mean treatment delay 3·7 h; 155 [18%] vs 112 [13%]; OR 1·56, 95% CI 1·17–2·08, p=0·0023; figure 2 )." Discussion: "we found no evidence that age modified either the proportional benefits or the proportional hazards of alteplase, with clear evidence of overall benefit for mRS 0–1 among the 1729 patients aged older than 80 years at randomisation." IST-3 abstract: "Benefit did not seem to be diminished in elderly patients." IST-3 abstract (primary outcome): "At 6 months, 554 (37%) patients in the rt-PA group versus 534 (35%) in the control group were alive and independent (OHS 0-2; adjusted odds ratio [OR] 1·13, 95% CI 0·95-1·35, p=0·181; a non-significant absolute increase of 14/1000, 95% CI -20 to 48). An ordinal analysis showed a significant shift in OHS scores"
claims.location: Emberson 2014 abstract and Results/Discussion (full-text excerpts); IST-3 abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: People with acute ischaemic stroke in 9 randomised trials (1729 aged over 80) / IV alteplase / placebo or open control / no significant disability (mRS 0-1) at 3 to 6 months
claims.safe_wording: In a combined analysis of 9 trials, 1729 people were over 80. Among them, about 18 in 100 given the clot-busting drug were left with no significant disability 3 to 6 months later, compared with about 13 in 100 who did not get it. The relative benefit was similar to that in younger people.
claims.qualifications: The over-80 figures pool all treatment delays in the trials (average 3.7 hours); benefit is larger the earlier treatment is given. In IST-3 alone, the main outcome (alive and independent at 6 months: 37 in 100 vs 35 in 100) did not show a clear difference; a secondary ordinal analysis did. Base the benefit statement on the meta-analysis, not on IST-3 alone.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: IST-3 authors warn that subgroup interactions, including apparently greater benefit over 80, should be interpreted with caution. People with severe pre-stroke disability or frailty were mostly excluded from trials (ESO).

claims.claim: Clot-busting treatment raises the early risk of bleeding into the brain, including fatal bleeding; overall this risk is outweighed by more people surviving without disability when given within 4.5 h.
claims.supporting_passage: Emberson abstract: "Alteplase significantly increased the odds of symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage (type 2 parenchymal haemorrhage definition 231 [6·8%] of 3391 vs 44 [1·3%] of 3365 ...) and of fatal intracranial haemorrhage within 7 days (91 [2·7%] vs 13 [0·4%]; OR 7·14, 95% CI 3·98-12·79, p<0·0001). The relative increase in fatal intracranial haemorrhage from alteplase was similar irrespective of treatment delay, age, or stroke severity, but the absolute excess risk attributable to alteplase was bigger among patients who had more severe strokes." ... "Taken together, therefore, despite an average absolute increased risk of early death from intracranial haemorrhage of about 2%, by 3-6 months this risk was offset by an average absolute increase in disability-free survival of about 10% for patients treated within 3·0 h and about 5% for patients treated after 3·0 h, up to 4·5 h." IST-3 abstract: "More deaths occurred within 7 days in the rt-PA group (163 [11%]) than in the control group (107 [7%] ...), but between 7 days and 6 months there were fewer deaths in the rt-PA group than in the control group, so that by 6 months, similar numbers, in total, had died (408 [27%] in the rt-PA group vs 407 [27%] in the control group)."
claims.pico_timeframe: People with acute ischaemic stroke / IV alteplase / control / symptomatic and fatal intracranial haemorrhage within 7 days; death and disability at 3-6 months
claims.safe_wording: The drug has a real risk: across the trials, about 3 in 100 people given it had a fatal bleed in the brain within a week, compared with fewer than 1 in 100 without it. Over the following months, more treated people survived without disability, when it was given within 4.5 hours of the stroke starting.
claims.qualifications: Give the harm as plainly as the benefit. The relative increase in fatal bleeding was similar at all ages. The net figures (about 10 more in 100 without disability if treated within 3 h, about 5 more in 100 at 3 to 4.5 h, against about 2 in 100 extra early deaths) are for all ages, not specifically over 80.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: In IST-3, early deaths were higher with alteplase (11% vs 7% at 7 days) but total deaths at 6 months were the same (27% vs 27%).

The exact wording of the life-expectancy phrase in the survey was not seen. Hypothetical scenario; US adults; stated preferences, not behaviour. A second survey found the same top and bottom choices in older adults with low health literacy (colonoscopy).

claims.claim: Many US older adults with limited life expectancy still receive cancer screening.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "Data from the population-based National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) from 2000 through 2010 were used and included 27 404 participants aged 65 years or older. Using a validated mortality index specific for NHIS, participants were grouped into those with low (<25%), intermediate (25%-49%), high (50%-74%), and very high (≥75%) risks of 9-year mortality." ... "In participants with very high mortality risk, 31% to 55% received recent cancer screening, with prostate cancer screening being most common (55%)." ... "Our sensitivity analysis showed that screening was also common in individuals with less than 5-year life expectancy."
claims.pico_timeframe: US adults 65+ in NHIS 2000-2010 / 9-year mortality risk groups / self-reported recent screening
claims.safe_wording: In US survey data from 2000 to 2010, among people aged 65 and over with at least a 75% chance of dying within 9 years, between about 1 in 3 and 1 in 2 had recently been screened for cancer, depending on the test.
claims.qualifications: US data to 2010, self-reported; the US screens opportunistically, unlike UK invitation programmes. Do not state UK screening ages (not verified from a document).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Rates may have changed since 2010.

numbers.meaning: survey participants aged 65+
recent screening among those with very high (>=75%) 9-year mortality risk, by cancer type
prostate screening in that group

claims.claim: Older adults were divided on whether life expectancy should be mentioned, so clinicians should still offer prognosis to people who want it.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "Third, participants preferred that clinicians explain a recommendation to stop screening by incorporating individual health status but were divided on whether life expectancy should be mentioned." Conclusions: "older adults may not consider life expectancy important in screening and may not prefer to hear about life expectancy when discussing screening."
claims.pico_timeframe: As C07-18-a
claims.safe_wording: People were divided on whether life expectancy should come up at all. Leading with health priorities and benefit does not mean hiding prognosis: offer it, and give it to people who want it.
claims.qualifications: The 'offer prognosis' instruction is a clinical and ethical judgement, supported only indirectly by the finding that people were divided; mark it as advice.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: After elective major abdominal surgery in people aged 60 and over, recovery of basic daily activities took on average about 3 months and of household and community activities about 6 months; some had not recovered by 6 months.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "This was a prospective cohort of 372 consecutive patients, 60 years old or more, enrolled from surgeons in private practice and two university-affiliated hospitals, assessed preoperatively and postoperatively at 1, 3, and 6 weeks, 3 and 6 months" ... "Mean age was 69 +/- 6 years" ... "Maximum functional declines (95% CI) occurred 1 week postoperatively" ... "Mean recovery times were: Mini-Mental State Exam, 3 weeks; timed walk, 6 weeks; ADL, SF-36 PCS, and functional reach, 3 months; and IADL, 6 months. Mean grip strength did not return to preoperative status by 6 months. The incidence of persistent disability at 6 months, compared with preoperative status, was: ADL, 9%; IADL, 19%" ... "Potentially modifiable independent predictors of ADL and IADL recovery were preoperative physical conditioning and depression plus serious postoperative complications."
claims.pico_timeframe: 372 consecutive US patients aged 60+ (mean 69) having elective major abdominal surgery / before vs after surgery / ADL, IADL and performance measures / up to 6 months
claims.safe_wording: In a US study of 372 people aged 60 and over having planned major abdominal operations, it took on average about 3 months to get back to their usual level of basic daily activities such as washing and dressing, and about 6 months for household tasks and getting out. At 6 months, about 1 in 10 had not recovered their basic daily activities and about 1 in 5 their household activities.
claims.qualifications: Elective abdominal surgery only, average age 69, 2004 (before widespread enhanced-recovery pathways); averages hide wide variation. Anchor 'three months' to this study and population; do not say it applies to all operations. ADL = basic daily activities (washing, dressing); IADL = household and community activities (shopping, cooking, managing money, transport).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Recovery may be faster with modern surgical care; no newer comparable study was checked in this batch.

mean age
mean time to recover basic daily activities (ADL)
mean time to recover household and community activities (IADL)
persistent ADL disability at 6 months

claims.claim: Most seriously ill older people who would accept a treatment that restored their current health said they would not choose it if the outcome was survival with severe functional or cognitive impairment.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "We administered a questionnaire about treatment preferences to 226 persons who were 60 years of age or older and who had a limited life expectancy due to cancer, congestive heart failure, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease." ... "For a low-burden treatment with the restoration of current health, 98.7 percent of participants said they would choose to receive the treatment (rather than not receive it and die), but 11.2 percent of these participants would not choose the treatment if it had a high burden. If the outcome was survival but with severe functional impairment or cognitive impairment, 74.4 percent and 88.8 percent of these participants, respectively, would not choose treatment." ... "The likelihood of adverse functional and cognitive outcomes of treatment requires explicit consideration."
claims.pico_timeframe: 226 US adults 60+ with limited life expectancy (cancer, heart failure, COPD) / hypothetical life-sustaining treatments with specified outcomes vs death / stated choice
claims.safe_wording: In a US study of 226 seriously ill people aged 60 and over, almost all would accept a simple treatment that kept them as they were. But about 3 in 4 said they would not choose it if it left them alive with severe physical disability, and about 9 in 10 if it left them with severe problems with thinking and memory.
claims.qualifications: Hypothetical scenarios where the alternative was death from their illness, not elective surgery; seriously ill US population in 2002. The 74.4% and 88.8% are among those who would accept the low-burden treatment (98.7%).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Stated preferences in scenarios may differ from real decisions.

numbers.meaning: seriously ill people aged 60+
would accept a low-burden treatment restoring current health
of these would not choose treatment if outcome was survival with severe functional impairment
of these would not choose treatment if outcome was survival with severe cognitive impairment

claims.claim: UK law (Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board, 2015) requires doctors to tell patients about material risks, judged by what a reasonable person in the patient's position, or this particular patient, would consider significant, and about reasonable alternatives.
claims.supporting_passage: Background: "In the UK these rights are affirmed by professional guidance [] and, since 2015, by the UK Supreme Court following the landmark decision of Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [] clarifying the nature of the relationship between healthcare professional (HCP) and patient on information disclosure." ... "By requiring a HCP to advise patients about alternatives and risks which may beto theirindividual circumstances it endorsed a patient's central role in decision-making." ... "The test of materiality is 'whether, in the circumstances of the particular case, a reasonable person in the patient's position would be likely to attach significance to the risk, or the doctor is or should reasonably be aware that the particular patient would be likely to attach significance to it [] (para 87). Whether a risk is regarded as material depends on the patient's perspective rather than the HCPs." Discussion: "Many legal cases have endorsed the duty to advise of 'reasonable' alternative care options".
claims.pico_timeframe: UK law on consent to treatment since 2015
claims.safe_wording: Since a 2015 UK Supreme Court ruling (Montgomery), doctors must tell you about any risk that a reasonable person in your position would think significant, or that they know or should know matters to you, and about reasonable alternatives. For many older people, not getting back to washing, dressing or living at home is exactly such a risk, so it is fair to ask about it.
claims.qualifications: Verified from a peer-reviewed secondary source quoting the judgment (para 87); the judgment and GMC guidance were not opened. Do not state that the law requires discussion of 'no treatment' specifically, or cite GMC wording. The sentence linking the test to recovery of daily function is an argument, not a legal ruling; mark it as such.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: year of the Montgomery Supreme Court judgment

claims.claim: Surgeons' descriptions of high-risk operations to older patients often focus on fixing the problem and on operative risks rather than on recovery.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "We observed surgeons who routinely perform high-risk surgery during preoperative discussions with patients. We used qualitative content analysis to explore the use of "fix-it" in 48 audio-recorded conversations." ... "Surgeons used the "fix-it" model for 2 separate purposes during preoperative conversations: (1) as an explanatory tool to facilitate patient understanding of disease and surgery, and (2) as a deliberation framework to assist in decision making. Although surgeons commonly used "fix-it" as an explanatory model, surgeons explicitly discussed limitations of the "fix-it" model as an independent rationale for operating as they deliberated about the value of surgery."
claims.pico_timeframe: 48 audio-recorded preoperative conversations, US surgeons doing high-risk surgery / qualitative
claims.safe_wording: In recorded US consultations before high-risk operations, surgeons commonly explained the operation as fixing the problem. The study did not measure whether recovery of daily life was discussed.
claims.qualifications: The abstract does not show that recovery was left out. Do not claim that consent discussions 'usually leave out' recovery of daily function; no source in this batch supports that for older surgical patients.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Surgeons also explicitly discussed the limits of the fix-it framing when weighing whether to operate.

numbers.meaning: audio-recorded preoperative conversations

candidates.reason: All essential claims are supported: IST-3 enrolment (3035; 1617, 53%, over 80, across both arms), historical exclusion of over-80s (IST-3 introduction, attributed; ESO), benefit in over-80s from the 9-trial individual patient data meta-analysis (18 vs 13 in 100 with no significant disability; similar relative benefit), the bleeding harm (fatal brain bleeding 2.7 vs 0.4 in 100 across ages), the ESO recommendation for over-80s with the consensus that age alone should not limit treatment, and time dependence (33 vs 23 in 100 within 3 h). Required wording: 'enrolled', not 'treated'; do not call IST-3 'the largest trial' without 'at the time (2012)'; base the benefit claim on the meta-analysis, because IST-3's own primary outcome (37 vs 35 in 100) was not significant; state the bleeding risk as plainly as the benefit; eligibility depends on time since onset and a brain scan (plus other criteria), not age; close on calling 999. The UK guideline's 'regardless of age' wording was seen only as a search extract (C07-30-g): cite European guidelines instead. Thrombectomy in over-80s (HERMES subgroup) is optional.

GAP70+ verified in full text: 718 people aged 70+ (mean 77) with incurable cancer and at least one impairment on geriatric assessment, starting a high-risk regimen in US community practices; grade 3 to 5 toxicity 177/349 (51%) vs 263/369 (71%); more reduced-dose starts, fewer falls (12 vs 21 in 100), more medicines stopped; survival similar at 6 months (72 vs 75 in 100) and 1 year, but the trial was not designed to show survival was unaffected, so avoid 'without shortening survival' as a proven claim. GAIN (605 aged 65+, 51 vs 61 in 100; no clear difference in admissions or survival) supports the finding. ASCO 2023 (US) recommends geriatric assessment for everyone over 65 with cancer. The UK line is supported by the SIOG UK group's 2024 review (only a small proportion can access specialist assessment); frame 'ask the cancer team' as advice. Note the ASCO erratum (2025, not reviewed).

Following the editor's guidance, the post keeps to cancer contact-day evidence and drops dialysis (C07-07-f, left to C07-24). Supported: the definition of contact days / time toxicity (CO.17 analysis; the 2022 JCO commentary was not opened, being closed access with no abstract); CO.17 medians of 28 vs 10 contact days (about 18% vs 6% of days alive) with no clear difference in home days (140 vs 121); the balancing result that in the KRAS wild-type group treatment gave more home days (186 vs 132) despite more contact days (41 vs 10); older adults with advanced cancer in US trials spent nearly 1 in 5 days in contact with health care (median 48 days in the first year; Mexican cohort 21%); and the omission of carers' time (authors' statement). Required: say CO.17's median age was 63; anchor the older-adult figure to Gupta 2025; include the home-days result so the post does not imply time-consuming treatment is never worth it; the claim that the same question applies to any treatment is the author's judgement and must not carry cancer percentages.

Supported with exact wording: the qualitative study (40 US adults aged 65+) found people open to stopping screening, and many found 'you may not live long enough to benefit from this test' unnecessarily harsh compared with 'this test would not help you live longer'. In the national survey (881 US adults aged 65+, hypothetical scenario), the most preferred explanation was 'your other health issues should take priority', the least preferred was 'the doctor does not give an explanation', and explanations mentioning life expectancy ranked low. The visual must NOT label the life-expectancy phrase as 'least preferred in the survey'. Use the interview pair for the harsh-versus-preferred contrast and the survey's most and least preferred phrases, which also shows that giving no explanation was liked least. Royce 2014 (US, to 2010) supports continued screening in people with limited life expectancy, if used. The line about offering prognosis is advice, supported by the finding that people were divided. US populations throughout; do not state UK screening ages.

Essential claims are supported only with qualifications, and one part of the angle is unsupported. Lawrence 2004 supports 'about 3 months' for basic daily activities and about 6 months for household and community activities, but only after elective major abdominal surgery in people aged 60 and over (mean 69, US, 2004); 1 in 10 still had lost basic activities and 1 in 5 household activities at 6 months. Fried 2002 supports that about 3 in 4 seriously ill older people would refuse treatment leading to severe functional impairment (hypothetical, US, n=226). The Montgomery materiality test and duty to discuss reasonable alternatives are verified from a secondary source quoting para 87; GMC guidance and a legal duty to discuss 'no treatment' were not verified. The core-insight claim that consent discussions 'usually leave out' recovery of daily life is not supported (Kruser 2015 shows only that surgeons commonly used a 'fix-it' explanation).
candidates.revised_angle: Present it as a question worth asking rather than a gap in practice: before a major operation, ask 'What is a normal day likely to look like at three months?' The reason is that recovery of daily activities often takes months: in a US study of planned major abdominal surgery in people over 60, basic self-care took about 3 months on average and household tasks about 6, and some never fully recovered. Add that many seriously ill older people weigh the chance of losing independence heavily (Fried, with its population), and that UK consent law asks doctors to discuss the risks this person would consider significant (Montgomery). Drop 'which consent usually leaves out' and GMC wording; the best case, worst case and most likely questions may stay as suggested questions.
